title: Three turns, twelve aspects
hook: each truth known, its task known, its task done: three turns of four truths (SN 56.11)
carry: no claim until all twelve are clear

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhāvetabba, to be developed, and your line, walk it. Did you take one step on the factor you chose? Today, the four truths and their tasks fit together into one shape. Day three hundred forty-four.

A checklist with three columns. Column one: do I know what this is? Column two: do I know what I'm supposed to do with it? Column three: have I actually done it? Plenty of lines in a life get the first tick and stall there. The test is whether every line gets all three. Near the end of his first sermon, the Buddha describes his own checklist, the one he ran through before he would say he was awakened. Four truths, three looks each. Today, the three turns and the twelve aspects.
screen: `A CHECKLIST, THREE COLUMNS.` → `THREE TICKS ON EVERY LINE.` → `THE BUDDHA'S OWN CHECKLIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the shape. For each of the four truths, the Buddha describes knowing it in three turns. The first turn: this is the truth. This is dukkha. The second turn: this is what's to be done with it. Dukkha is to be understood. The third turn: it has been done. Dukkha has been understood. Then the same three for the cause: this is the arising; it's to be let go; it has been let go. For the ending: this is the ending; it's to be realized; it has been realized. For the path: this is the path; it's to be developed; it has been developed. Four truths times three turns: twelve aspects. And then the striking line. The Buddha tells the five monks that as long as his knowledge of these three turns and twelve aspects wasn't fully clear, he didn't claim to be awakened. Only when all twelve were clear did he say it. That's honesty about his own path, built right into the first sermon. Then the story turns. As the sermon ends, one of the five, Kondañña, sees it. The sutta says the clear vision arose in him that whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease. And the Buddha says, Kondañña has understood. That, the sutta says, is how he got the name Aññasi Kondañña, Kondañña who understood. The sutta says the gods of the earth shouted that the wheel had been set rolling, and the cry passed up through the heavens. Some teachers today use the twelve as a map: knowing a truth, knowing its task, and doing it are three different things.
screen: `THIS IS. TO BE DONE. DONE.` · `FOUR TIMES THREE: TWELVE.` · `NO CLAIM UNTIL ALL TWELVE.` · `KONDAÑÑA UNDERSTOOD.` · then, large: `THREE TURNS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to write out the twelve. If you have paper, draw a grid: four rows for the four truths, three columns, this is, to be done, done. Fill in the first two columns as you breathe. Leave the third column empty, or put a light mark where you've had even a small taste. If you have no paper, walk the grid in your mind, one box per breath. No grading. Just the shape. The bell holds the time.
Three turns. Each of the four truths known three ways: this is it, this is what's to be done, it has been done. Twelve aspects in all.

Your line: no claim until all twelve are clear. Today, pick one thing you know you should do, and notice which turn you're on: knowing it, knowing what to do, or having done it. Day three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: The first sermon, with its three turns and twelve aspects, is often chanted in Pali in Theravada monasteries, especially on Asalha Puja, and some teachers use the twelve as a map of practice.

match.prompt: match each turn to what it says.
pairs: this is what's to be done

he says he didn't claim it until all three turns of all four truths were fully clear.

fork.setup: the sermon ends. one of the five listeners has seen it. what does the sutta say he saw?
options: that the Buddha was a god.
that whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease.
that the world will end soon.
fork.reveal: Kondañña saw that whatever arises is subject to ceasing, and the Buddha said: Kondañña has understood.

original.note: Pali tiparivaṭṭa: three turns or rounds; the first sermon's three turns of knowing for each truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: knowing the four truths means being able to list them.
what it means: each truth is known three ways: as true, as a task, and as a task done.
what a scholar hears: SN 56.11 calls this tiparivaṭṭa dvādasākāra, three turns and twelve aspects, and only then does the Buddha claim anuttara sammāsambodhi.

sources.ref: SN 56.11 (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta), the three turns and twelve aspects; Kondañña's insight

notes: SN 56.11 paraphrased: confirm the order of the three turns, the claim that awakening was not declared until all twelve were clear, Kondañña's vision (yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamman ti), and the cry of the earth devas rising through the heavens.
